Global media critiques Ramayana film & the great expectations in a ‘politically charged moment in India’

China's Global Times comments on growing debate over Beijing's export controls on tunnel boring machines.

Prakhar Agrawal

New Delhi: The epic tale of Ram and Sita is back in the spotlight in India’s most expensive film to date.

BBC delves into the enduring hold of the Ramayana as Namit Malhotra and Nitesh Tiwari bring it back to the big screen..

The film may have received mixed reviews, but has turned heads within India and outside nonetheless.

Show Full Article

Meanwhile, China’s Global Times comments on the growing debate over Beijing’s export controls on tunnel boring machines, and the India link.

Also Read: Can India establish a viable semiconductor industry? Global media says ‘success is far from guaranteed’

I n a report for the BBC , Zoya Mateen looks at the release of Part 1 of Ramayana: Rise of a Legend , and the expectations surrounding its attempt to take one of Hinduism’s foundational epics to a global audience. Directed by Nitesh Tiwari, the film has critics divided over whether its VFX-laden visual spectacle does justice to the story.

But the film’s significance goes beyond its critical reception. In India, the film—starring Ranbir Kapoor, Sai Pallavi and Yash—has invited comparisons with earlier adaptations, especially Ramanand Sagar’s Ramayan , which “captivated the country nearly four decades ago with simple sets and special effects that now seem quaint”.

When the television series first aired in 1987, it became a national phenomenon. “Streets emptied, shops lowered their shutters and neighbours crowded around TV sets. Some viewers bathed, lit incense and garlanded their screens before the broadcast, preparing for the show much as they might for worship,” Mateen writes.

Arvind Rajagopal, a media scholar at New York University, told the BBC in 2019 that “trains and buses would stop and passengers disembark to watch the show on roadside TVs”.

The report also recalls the 1992 Indian-Japanese animated film Ramayana: The Legend of Prince Rama , which brought the epic to life through richly detailed, hand-drawn animation. The film was an Indian-Japanese collaboration, combining an Indian epic with Japanese animation techniques and storytelling traditions.

“Tiwari’s Ramayana arrives with technological resources its predecessors could barely have imagined—but also with the expectations of generations who have grown up with the story and its characters,” Mateen adds.

The expectations are not just cultural, but also political. “It also comes at a politically charged moment in India, where Ram has become a powerful symbol of Hindu identity—over the past decade and a half, even popular analyses or retellings of the epic have landed in controversy.” The 2023 film Adipurush —another big-budget retelling of the Ramayana, starring Prabhas, Kriti Sanon and Saif Ali Khan—had sparked backlash over its portrayal of religious figures, dialogue and visual effects.

Meanwhile, writing in The Guardian , Peter Bradshaw calls the newly released Ramayana a “thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular Indian epic melodrama”. He found echoes of Shakespeare in the royal intrigue that sends Ram into exile, and of Homer in his quest to rescue Sita, Mateen notes.

But Siddhant Adlakha of IGN was not so impressed. He scored the film four out of 10. For him, the action sequences were “clunky” and the computer-generated imagery (CGI) an “eye-sore”.

The use of AI to adjust lip movements of actors for the English version has also been criticised. For Tiwari, the idea was to make the film more accessible to international viewers, BBC report adds, but Adlakha describes it as “exaggerated mouth movements superimposed on still images for comedy sketches”.

The report also captures the weight of the roles for the actors. Ranbir Kapoor, who plays Ram, told the BBC that he was “filled with fear”, playing Lord Ram on the big screen.

How the film is received will become clearer as audiences head to cinemas. “But whatever the verdict, it marks a major cultural moment for India, bringing a story loved for generations to the big screen on an unprecedented scale,” Mateen writes.

Also Read: Reliance bet on diversification, and it paid off. But margins may ‘prove difficult to sustain’—global media

I n an editorial titled ‘A single TBM should not become a source of friction between China and India’, the Global Times responds to the debate over China’s export controls on tunnel boring machines, arguing that the issue should not become another source of tension between New Delhi and Beijing.

India’s Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal recently said that if China did not supply TBMs, India would develop them domestically, insisting that “India is not one to bow down”. The remarks received coverage in Indian and Western media, with several portraying the issue as “India refusing to yield to China’s ‘chokehold’”.

China announced the export controls on 19 October, with measures due to take effect on 18 November.

The editorial clarifies that the announcement “does not name any country”, and that the controls “are not directed at any specific party”. It stresses that “the measures centre on licensing rather than an outright export ban”. Applications for compliant exports to legitimate civilian projects, it says, will be approved provided the end users and end uses are clearly identified and meet the relevant requirements.

Global Times acknowledges, “India may have some misunderstandings or even complaints about these measures, and that is understandable”. It points out that “the country is in the midst of an intensive infrastructure-building drive”, and that, whether for metro networks, high-speed rail projects, highways or water conservancy tunnels, “India has considerable demand for large-scale excavation equipment such as TBMs”.

However, it argues that “there is little need to politicise a routine export-control matter”, let alone turn it into a question of whether India will “never bow down”, or defend its “national dignity”. Dismissing speculation that China is deliberately seeking to “restrict India’s use of TBMs in border areas”, the editorial says such claims “say more about the insecurity of those making them than about China’s intentions”.

It warns that “a confrontational mindset will only narrow the space for pragmatic consultations, ultimately jeopardising India’s own infrastructure projects and development progress”.

At the same time, it says India’s pursuit of “self-reliance” and efforts to build domestic TBM manufacturing capabilities are legitimate aspirations, while China has “an equally legitimate right to safeguard its national security and fulfill its international obligations”. Global Times adds: “China has never viewed India’s development as a threat to itself.” It also insists that “China is not that ‘petty’”.

Taking aim at Western coverage, the Global Times says certain US media outlets have shown particular “enthusiasm” for the issue. It mentions Bloomberg ‘s description of the export controls as “a trade war risk to India”, while accusing The New York Times of portraying China’s industrial strengths as a “source of economic leverage” and claiming that “Beijing was building up its arsenal of economic weapons”.

The editorial further argues that such coverage seeks to “drive a wedge between China and India”, urging the two countries to address the issue through technical channels, rather than allow it to undermine broader bilateral relations.

(Edited by Mannat Chugh)

India ranks 11th in Commonwealth youth AI readiness index

The study is published by the Ayre Think Tank, which is affiliated with the Calvin Ayre Foundation.

Romal Renny

06 November, 2026 01:34 pm IST

Follow Us:

New Delhi: India has ranked 11th among 56 Commonwealth countries in the 2026 Commonwealth Youth AI Readiness Index, with a score of 60.6 out of 100.

The study estimates that artificial intelligence could increase India’s GDP by approximately $79.1 billion over 10 years under a moderate-growth scenario, giving it the second-largest potential economic gain among Commonwealth nations.

Published by the Ayre Think Tank, which is affiliated with the Calvin Ayre Foundation, the index examines how prepared young people aged 15 to 29 are to benefit from artificial intelligence. It draws on 1,128 research sources and assesses countries across areas including digital access, education, employment, enterprise and AI safeguards.

Show Full Article

The study sets a readiness benchmark of 53, with 15 countries meeting or exceeding it.

India’s youth population and AI adoption India’s large youth population is a significant factor in its AI readiness. The report estimates that approximately 382 million Indians are aged between 15 and 29, accounting for more than half of the Commonwealth’s 732 million young people.

The study also found considerable enthusiasm for AI among young Indians. According to the survey data examined by researchers, 88.8 per cent expected to use AI for education or work within the following year, while 60.1 per cent said they were confident in their ability to control their interactions with the technology.

However, gaps in digital access and employment remain significant challenges. Although India has widespread 4G coverage and relatively inexpensive mobile data, only 66.5 per cent of young people were found to own a mobile phone.

The report also found that 30.4 per cent of young people were not in employment, education or training, while 85.8 per cent of young workers were employed informally.

Also read: Anthropic study’s new AI cautionary tale: AI agents can influence expert opinion to serve bias

AI could add up to $119 billion to GDP The study outlines three possible scenarios for AI’s economic impact on India over the next 10 years.

Under the conservative estimate, AI could increase the country’s GDP by $39.6 billion. The moderate scenario puts the figure at $79.1 billion, while the optimistic estimate reaches $118.7 billion.

These figures represent potential changes in GDP levels after 10 years, rather than annual growth or guaranteed economic gains.

Calvin Ayre, founder of the Ayre Think Tank, said the benefits of AI would depend on whether young people had the skills and opportunities to participate in the changing economy.

“What matters is giving young people the skills and the chance to get ahead – whether to start businesses, find jobs or build something for themselves,” he said in a statement to PR Newswire Canada.

Government initiatives and priorities   The findings come as the Indian government expands its AI skills initiatives. Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced plans in August 2026 to train 10 million youth in AI skills within a year. In September, the government also launched training programmes in partnership with Intel India.

The report identifies five priorities for improving youth AI readiness: affordable and reliable digital access; practical, skills-based education; better pathways from training to employment; AI tools adapted to local languages and needs; and safeguards that allow young people to question automated decisions.

(Edited by Maryam Hassan)

The republic against its president

Americans have repudiated the Trump administration's performance, but not necessarily Trumpism itself. An election cannot, by itself, repair institutions or reverse years of political mistrust.

Swasti Rao

06 November, 2026 10:00 am IST

Follow Us:

-->

4

Facebook

X

LinkedIn

Email

Copy Link

File photo of President Donald Trump addressing a joint session of Congress at the US Capitol on in Washington, DC | Win McNamee | Pool via Reuters

T he American midterms have reopened an argument older than the United States itself: how does a democracy protect its liberties from the personal ambitions of those elected to govern it? The question belongs to every democracy, even if the consequences of America’s experience travel unusually far and wide.

Trump has not lost the presidency; his party has lost Congress. The distinction is considerable and hardly promises a sea change in America’s conduct abroad. Still, the scale of the Republican defeat is stunning. Democrats have won both chambers , with gains extending into territory long considered unshakeably Republican. Texas and Kansas stand out. Since much has already been written about how those electoral tables turned, you, dear reader, will gain little from me recounting them again.

More interesting is the return of an older constitutional argument. The American presidency, perhaps the most powerful elected executive office in the modern world, was never designed to exercise authority without institutional restraint. During the first two years of Trump’s second term, Congress had been forced to accommodate brute presidential power. However, the midterms have restored the genuine possibility of a Congress willing to act independently of the president.

Show Full Article

Also Read: Israel must now decide what kind of democracy it wants to be

Old suspicion of sovereign power More than eight centuries ago, Magna Carta of 1215 placed an enduring proposition into writing: the English king too, it said, was subject to law. It was the outcome of a confrontation between King John and his barons, and not a declaration of universal political rights per se. But the political ideas that arose from Magna Carta have been far more expansive than the immediate quarrel that produced it.

A few centuries later, the struggles between Crown and Parliament, the English Bill of Rights of 1689 and the political philosophy of John Locke gradually developed the case for limited government. The French philosopher Montesquieu gave that argument an institutional form. In The Spirit of the Laws (1748), he warned against placing the powers to legislate, execute and judge in the same hands. That principle travelled into revolutionary France: Article 16 of the 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen treated the separation of powers as indispensable to a democratic constitution.

The American founders carried this same suspicion of concentrated authority into their own constitutional deliberations. Among them was James Madison , a young Virginian who arrived at the Philadelphia Convention of 1787 exceptionally well prepared. He had studied ancient and European confederations for clues to the weaknesses of political unions. He went on to become one of the American Constitution’s principal architects, a chronicler of the convention’s debates and, eventually, America’s fourth president.

Madison had little faith in the proposition that good government could be secured simply by choosing good men. In Federalist No. 51 , he offered the more durable prescription that “ambition must be made to counteract ambition.” The American president would possess formidable authority, but Congress would legislate and control expenditure; courts would decide constitutional disputes; and federalism would distribute power between Washington and the states. The institutions were expected to compete, disagree and occasionally frustrate one another. That was how the republic was meant to function, frustrating as it may be. That was the plan from the get-go.

For all these arrangements, the early American republic was far from perfect. Its constitutional settlement accommodated slavery, excluded women from political participation and left large sections of the population without an effective vote. The Nineteenth Amendment secured women’s voting rights only in 1920. Even a century after the emancipation of enslaved African Americans during the Civil War, discriminatory laws and intimidation still kept many Black citizens from the ballot, until the Voting Rights Act of 1965 sought to dismantle those barriers.

The republic’s distinction, therefore, rested not on an immaculate beginning but in a constitutional framework that allowed the struggle for citizenship, representation and equality to continue. Its institutions were conceived to outlast the ambitions and shortcomings of individuals, including presidents.

Peculiar illiberalism of contemporary populism Over the past decade, constitutional democracy has encountered a peculiar challenge to its institutions, simultaneously internal and external. Political movements gain legitimacy through elections and then question the legitimacy of the restraints that make elected government constitutional. An institution is then not criticised for a particular failing; it is denounced as part of an elite arrangement supposedly hostile to the people. If that has not rung a bell yet, I am referring to the rise of populist politics across the world.

The language of the populist, ‘anti-woke’ revolt has made this accusation especially convenient. Judicial independence, minority protections, procedural safeguards, the autonomy of public institutions and even independent journalism can be easily dismissed as components of a liberal-left agenda. In the process, liberal constitutionalism is reduced to a partisan label, as though limits on arbitrary authority had been invented by contemporary progressives for their personal benefit.

That is a remarkable historical inversion. The principle that public power must be limited has a distinguished conservative inheritance, from the English constitutional tradition to American republicanism. A disagreement with a court’s ruling or a newspaper’s editorial line is perfectly legitimate. The claim that either institution is inherently an enemy of the people because it refuses political obedience is something else altogether.

MAGA turned this distinction into a central political battleground. The movement’s rhetoric of the “deep state” supplies an all-weather, all-purpose explanation for delegitimising opposition, while Trump’s electoral mandate has been treated as authority to override institutional checks. The violent breach of the Capitol on 6 January 2021 supplied an extreme demonstration of what happens when electoral defeat itself is interpreted as evidence that democratic institutions have betrayed the people.

Trump has exploited this notion with remarkable élan and consistency. His attempts to extend executive discretion, challenge limits on congressionally authorised spending and demand loyalty from institutions expected to exercise independent judgement have encouraged a personalised understanding of his presidency. Freedom of courts is recast as adversarial; administrative restraint becomes disobedience and congressional oversight is framed as sabotage. The distance between MAGA’s conception of political authority and Madison’s constitutional republic could scarcely be starker.

Trump did not create the powerful American presidency, nor has he made it all-powerful. But he has tested how much of the constitutional system depends upon the willingness of institutions, and the people within them, to defend their prerogatives. The midterms have exposed a serious political limit to that experiment. Whether or not they also restore an institutional limit remains to be seen.

Congress, the inconvenient institution The Democrats’ victory will alter this relationship, though not necessarily in the ways those celebrating it expect. Their substantial majority gives congressional leaders more room to organise investigations, control committees, examine expenditure and resist presidential nominations.

Yet a majority is not omnipotence. Trump retains his veto, which requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers to override. Most of the contested legislation in the Senate must also clear the 60-vote threshold for ending debate. Congress, on its part, can constrain presidential initiatives more readily than it can impose a comprehensive alternative programme. Congress retains substantial oversight of war and foreign affairs, but the president remains commander-in-chief and holds considerable diplomatic and operational discretion.

There is another question for the Republicans. Congress was not constitutionally helpless during the first part of Trump’s second term, but Republican legislators frequently chose accommodation over scrutiny. The electorate has now changed that political calculation. The defeat of Trump-endorsed Vivek Ramaswamy in Ohio, alongside Republican losses elsewhere, weakens the assumption that fidelity to MAGA guarantees electoral success. JD Vance’s unusually explicit criticism of the Iran war right after the Republican defeat has already raised questions about the movement’s future.

The next Congress will be in a much better position to demand accountability from Trump. Whether Democrats can exercise that authority without allowing legislative conflict to harden into permanent paralysis is a separate challenge. A republic needs checks on executive power, but it also needs a government capable of making decisions and functioning.

Also Read: US midterms have created conditions to tame Superman Trump

Morning after America’s domestic politics have an unusually large international audience. The country’s economic and financial dominance, the dollar’s status as the world’s principal reserve currency, and its military, technological and diplomatic reach connect Washington’s choices to the fortunes of countries far beyond its borders. What happens in Vegas may stay in Vegas. What happens in Washington seldom does.

For Vladimir Putin, a Democratic Congress could mean stronger scrutiny of American policy toward Russia and greater pressure to assist Ukraine. European allies may find more receptive interlocutors on Capitol Hill. International far-right movements (like Germany’s AfD), encouraged by MAGA and even by the administration’s 2025 National Security Strategy, may have to reconsider the political value of association with Trump. However, the domestic grievances sustaining right-wing populism have not disappeared with an American midterm election.

The immediate test is Iran. The war played a role in costing Republicans their congressional majorities, and it is tempting to assume that defeat might compel a retreat. However, what seems more plausible is that Trump may delay renewed escalation or find an added incentive to negotiate longer. He has defended the original intervention, and there is little evidence yet that the larger course of his policy has changed. A weakened president may seek a way out, but Trump may also double down in pursuit of an outcome he can present as his legacy. Congress can complicate his choices, but not force him to retreat. And that will carry implications for everyone caught in the crossfire of energy disruptions, including India.

Nor does a Democratic sweep necessarily promise functional government. The coming two years could bring rigorous oversight and useful compromise, but they could equally bring vetoes, budgetary deadlock and greater reliance on unilateral executive action. That possibility is not an indictment of the separation of powers but a reminder that constitutional machinery still requires political judgement.

Americans have repudiated the administration’s performance, but it would be premature to declare that they have repudiated every idea associated with Trumpism. An election cannot, by itself, repair institutions or reverse years of political mistrust.

Trump promised to make America great again. He has, for the moment, made it blue again. The harder question is whether America’s political stakeholders can now make it functional again.

Swasti Rao is a Consulting Editor (International and Strategic Affairs) at ThePrint. She tweets @swasrao. Views are personal.

(Edited by Asavari Singh)
